pr_title: Add indexed column support to Windows users table
pr_body:
Fixes #6411 by advertising and implementing an index on the `uuid` column of the `users` table on Windows, allowing for `JOIN` operations with linear performance instead of exponential.

Although `uid` is the indexed column on POSIX systems, I went with the `uuid` column since it holds SIDs, the preferred (?) unique identifier for Windows users.

- [x] Should the `uid` column also implement an index?

Caveat: I'm not a Windows user so I cannot speak about the correct approach.

Implementing an index on UID will allow generic queries to apply to all platforms.

> Caveat: I'm not a Windows user so I cannot speak about the correct approach.
> 
> Implementing an index on UID will allow generic queries to apply to all platforms.

That's true. Ok I'll try, and if it's possible to look up a Windows user by UID then I'll add indexing to that column to this PR.

> Though I also wonder if we need to be using `dwUserInfoLevel = 3`

I will address your other points, but yea, I don't know why the original code needed to fill a "USER_INFO_3" struct and then make another call to just get the same data in a "USER_INFO_4" struct, since the 4 struct supersedes the 3 struct on Windows XP and newer, which is all we care about. I'll see if a single API can accomplish what's needed here.

Update: Ok, it is the behavior of the APIs that you can only request level 3 info from `NetUserEnum`. The documentation says you cannot get level 4 info from this API, and indeed on trying it, it returns `ERROR_INVALID_LEVEL`. I'll leave a code comment to clarify that this was written as intended.

I'll work on refactoring the code redundancy here next.

> I know this is just a draft... But I'd like to see the `uid` and the `*` paths use the same underlying functions.
> 
> Right now, `processLocalAccounts` calls `NetUserEnum` and then calls `NetUserGetInfo`.
> 
> Whereas, `genUser` calls `LookupAccountSidW`. and has a lot of general duplication.
> 
> I'd generally expect to have a specified user bypass the `NetUserEnum` call.

To summarize how it works today: the table gets a `*` query and has to enumerate users. It does so with a loop around `NetUserEnum`/`NetUserGetInfo` (the `processLocalAccounts` routine that collects local-only accounts, followed by a walk of the Profiles key in the Registry (a list of SIDs) to retrieve domain-accounts that have logged in locally (not found with `NetUserEnum`) (the `processRoamingProfiles` routine). The latter routine, given a SID, completes the information using `LookupAccountSidW`, but the former routine, having no information about the users it wants, has to use `NetUserEnum`, and then it still has no SID so it has to use `NetUserGetInfo` at which point there's no need to call `LookupAccountSidW` since it has everything it needs.

If the table gets a constraint of `uuid` (which is the SID) then it can skip directly to calling `LookupAccountSidW` and that's what I do in this PR. If the table gets a constraint of `uid` (an incomplete SID, actually the suffix of a SID aka the RID) then what I plan to do is, in the loop that enumerates all the users, skip row generation if the `uid` doesn't match the user's RID. This will be a big speedup but not as big as if the user provides full SIDs using `uuid` so that no enumeration has to be done.

While it looks like parallel implementations of getting user data, they're not redundant, and I don't think they can be combined. There could still be room for improvement to this old code, but I mainly wanted to make this table usable for JOINs on Windows because several user have been asking for it.

```
PS C:\Projects\osquery\build> .\osquery\RelWithDebInfo\osqueryi.exe "select chrome_extensions.name, chrome_extensions.description, chrome_extensions.version, users.username from chrome_extensions left join users ON chrome_extensions.uid=users.uid;"                             W1208 18:52:44.689471  1784 virtual_table.cpp:961] The chrome_extensions table returns data based on the current user by default, consider JOINing against the users table
```

This is where it's at currently. I _think_ this is implemented the way it needs to be.

You can still get disastrous performance if you phrase the query the other way: `select * from users JOIN chrome_extensions USING (uid);` because it will enumerate the whole `users` table for each row in the `chrome_extensions` table. Isn't that expected though? (Note: I am using the implementation of chrome_extensions from the master branch, not the one Alessandro has rewritten.)

Speculating on performance.... If I assume a common use case is a join to get very basic user info, and you can identify which columns a query is using, you can probably call an appropriate info level in the loop, and skip `USER_INFO_4` fill in. (might be better left for future work)

> Speculating on performance.... If I assume a common use case is a join to get very basic user info, and you can identify which columns a query is using, you can probably call an appropriate info level in the loop, and skip `USER_INFO_4` fill in. (might be better left for future work)

If I can follow an existing table that implements this precedent (generating only some columns of a row in response to a query for just those columns) then I could maybe do that. Otherwise, this PR implements the acceptable `JOIN` performance and improves the speed of each loop iteration, which are both good enough reasons for a merge if others agree.

I agree. The suggestion to optimize based on columns is not blocking. This is clearly much better than status quo.
Thanks for testing on Darwin, I agree with the other reviewers and I think we can merge.

issue_context.title: Severe memory and performance issues when joining users table
issue_context.body:
<!-- Thank you for contributing to osquery! -->

# Bug report

<!--
Please follow this template.
Before submitting an issue search for duplicates.
-->

### What operating system and version are you using?

Windows Server 2016

<!--
You can run the command bellow. Paste result within a code block.

osqueryi --line "SELECT version, build, platform FROM os_version;"
-->

### What version of osquery are you using?

osqueryi (shell) 3.3.2, 4.1.2, and 4.3.0

<!--
You can run the line bellow. Paste the result within a code block.

osqueryi --line "SELECT version from osquery_info;"
-->

### What steps did you take to reproduce the issue?

Run the following query from a high-user count system:
- E.g., domain controller server with large number of domain users
- or any machine with large number of local users.

> SELECT * FROM users JOIN chrome_extensions USING (uid);

### What did you expect to see?

Timely results, reasonable memory usage.

### What did you see instead?

No results (pretty sure osquery crashed), took 8 days to run before crashing, extremely high memory usage (~11/16 GB used at peak, averaging ~7GB over 8 days).

The domain controller server in question services ~100K accounts.  Expectation was that the users table would include local accounts, but long run time and memory usage suggest that all accounts on the domain were being enumerated.  Regardless of enumeration behavior, the run time and memory usage was extremely debilitating to the server and the machines that rely on it.

Looking through the users table Windows code, the [NetUserEnum call that drives the enumeration](https://github.com/osquery/osquery/blob/master/osquery/tables/system/windows/users.cpp#L125) is using a filter value of 0, which may be causing the domain enumeration; I am curious if FILTER_NORMAL_ACCOUNT would make the enum more targeted to avoid over-enumeration.

Testing with osqueryi 3.3.2, 4.1.2, and 4.3.0 on local non-server VMs that have 10,000 local accounts demonstrates similar behavior.  The query has been running for several hours now, using a significant amount of memory.

> SELECT * FROM users;

does not result in unreasonably long run duration or high memory usage on these test VMs.  It seems to be only when joining the chrome_extensions and users tables.  I imagine joining users with other tables may have the same effect.

Two main points:

- It's not clear if the users table should include all domain users, notably in this case where the query is run on a domain controller server.  If it is intended, this doesn't seem like desirable behavior for large domains.
- There is a major performance and resource issue with queries that involve joining with the users table when there are a large number of users that osquery can query.
comments:
Nice catch!

This can be explained by the fact that while the users table spec says that `uid` is an index, the Windows implementation of that table doesn't support that column to be an index and so it doesn't optimize the query based on it.
When a column is an index and a JOIN is done on it, what is expected is that the table will do an optimization and only search and return that column value because for each row to JOIN sqlite will call the table row generation, so it got to be fast; instead here everytime the table generation code is called, all the users are retrieved and almost all then discarded later by sqlite, because only one uid is really needed.

As for querying users on a domain, I was aware too that doing network calls of that type should be avoided or at least maybe they should be behind a special column/differently named table.

This PowerShell script creates an arbitrary number of user accounts (disabled with no password, but usable for testing).
https://gist.github.com/mike-myers-tob/1f30c1f0ba994b31d9f7c3cd40bf50ee

In the gist I've included the link to a 100,000 row CSV, to create that many new local user accounts. This actually works on Windows 10 Pro. They're not domain accounts. As @tferguson7337 said, they'll still have performance issues with `JOIN` but I'll need a different VM to set up a bunch of Domain users.

The CPU usage on a 3-core Windows 10 Pro VM never exceeded 25%, and memory overhead fluctuated around 50MB.

As @Smjert pointed out, the table needs to implement the "index" on the `UUID` column; otherwise it's true that `JOIN` operations get out of hand. I'm working on that too.

review_comments: Actually I think this `if`/`else` setup is fine? If one did an early `return` here you'd have two `return` statements. Left as is we always update `results` and have the single return at the end. Thoughts?

Hrm. I'm generally okay with multiple returns. At least, I find it cleaner than parsing nested if blocks.

But I also don't think we should block on style here
If I may be the tiebreaker opinion then, I'd like to leave it this way, and it's a short routine anyway.
